title: Geo penalty routing, quantization impact, and VPC DR drill
summary: SE-led deep dive on geo-penalty routing weights, how quantization profiles affect tail latency and throughput, and a proposed VPC/on-prem DR drill with KV warmstart strategies. Agreed next steps: run a two-region canary with penalize-scoring, provide a latency/cost tradeoff matrix for int8 vs 4-bit quant, and share a DR runbook draft with warmup scripts.
topics: KV cache warmstart and eviction strategy
VPC on-prem DR runbook and simulation plan
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-18 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~72 mins | Recording: Fireflies auto
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Soto (Redwood Solutions), Elena Marquez (CTO, StrataScale), Tom Reid (Platform Eng), Priya Anand (SRE), Luis Ortega (Security)

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda—geo-penalty routing approach, quantization effects on our latency SLOs, KV warmstart and eviction, and then the VPC DR drill we sketched last week.
00:12 Elena: sounds good, trying to keep this focused — we have a holiday load coming and want to avoid cross-region blips.
00:20 Maya: cool, I'll start with the routing policy idea then Ravi will cover cache warmstart and quantization numbers.
00:30 Maya: So, at a high level, geo-penalty routing applies a small latency penalty to cross-region candidates so sticky sessions prefer local regions unless capacity constraints force a fallback. It's a soft penalty, not hard-affinity. We compute a score: base_score = latency_ms * weight_latency + penalty_geo + model_cost_score and choose lowest.
00:55 Tom: when you say "penalty_geo" is that a fixed ms add or a multiplier?
01:01 Maya: good Q — we support both. For StrataScale use-case we recommend an additive ms penalty (e.g., +25ms) for cross-region; multipliers are more aggressive and can destabilize during surges.
01:17 Priya: can we do dynamic adjust — like increase penalty when egress cost thresholds breached?
01:23 Maya: absolutely — policy can reference cost signals and scale penalty. We also can pin critical customers to dedicated capacity to avoid that decision entirely.
01:34 Jordan: important to note the penalty shouldn't be too large; otherwise the routing will keep failing over to saturated local nodes and increase queueing latency.
01:45 Elena: that was our concern: local saturation + sticky sessions caused a slow degradation last Q.
01:50 Ravi: on the cache side — KV warmstart. We profiled a cold start sequence: when a cold region receives traffic after failover, cold KV cache leads to a 2–3x increase in tail latency for first few minutes because KV misses cause whole prefix recompute.
02:10 Ravi: mitigation: pre-warm by seeding popular prefixes and using background async replication of hot keys across regions. We provide an export tool to snapshot top-N prefixes and a worker to rehydrate in target region before traffic shift.
02:29 Tom: do you stream updates continuously or snapshot?
02:32 Ravi: hybrid. Snapshot top-N every hour plus stream deltas for hot keys. For low-churn prefixes snapshot is fine. For LLM session KV we prefer streaming for safety.
02:45 Priya: what about cache coherence and correctness — do you risk serving stale KV that harms responses?
02:51 Maya: we tag cache entries with last-updated TTL and model-compatibility hash; fallback is to fetch remote KV during request if mismatch is detected. There's a small latency cost but better than serving broken continuations.
03:10 Luis: security question — replication across regions, does that leak data residency? We have PII in some prompts.
03:18 Jordan: good call — for regulated workflows we suggest not replicating KV containing PII. Instead, either keep those sessions in dedicated region or use encryption + access controls and audit logs. We'll share our KMS/HSM integration details.
03:30 Maya: quick segue to batching and burst shapes. Continuous batching helps throughput but increases tail for small request percentiles. For StrataScale we saw 95th percentile spikes when batching window grew above 8ms under bursty arrivals.
03:46 Ravi: so our recommendation is adaptive batching: max batch latency 6ms under normal load, auto-drop to 2ms when queue depth is low, and increase batch size during sustained throughput. This keeps latency SLOs while preserving cost.
04:05 Tom: do you have numbers for quantization impact? We're exploring int8 and 4-bit for cost reasons.
04:10 Maya: yes — high-level: int8 (symmetric) yields ~1.6–2x throughput improvement on GPU kernels with 5–8% quality delta on some tasks; 4-bit (QLoRA-style) can get 2.8–3.5x throughput but quality regression varies more — often fine for summarization but risky for instruction fidelity.
04:33 Ravi: tail latency wise, quantized kernels reduce per-token time but can suffer from jitter because some model paths fall back to FP ops for certain ops (e.g., gated activations). We instrument kernel fallback and it's rare but causes a 20–80ms spike on affected tokens.
04:52 Elena: that's concerning for our 150ms 95th SLO.
04:56 Maya: we propose a mixed strategy: run hot routes in int8, keep critical customer tiers or low-latency endpoints in higher-precision. Also Canary quant profiles in a dedicated canary region to capture regressions.
05:15 Jordan: combine that with geo-penalty scoring: penalize quantized variants slightly for endpoints that require deterministic output quality; routing can choose int8 variant only if score meets threshold.
05:28 Tom: ok that makes sense. Now on DR drill — Priya, you had a runbook idea?
05:33 Priya: yea, we drafted a 7-step drill: 1) telemetry baseline capture, 2) synthetic warmup of hot prefixes in target region, 3) switch 20% traffic via penalty policy, 4) escalate to 100% if healthy, 5) run KV reconciliation job, 6) validate end-to-end correctness, 7) rollback.
05:50 Ravi: important nuance — step 2 must seed KV with session continuity markers so reunion doesn't produce hallucinations. The warmup worker can do prefix-writes and mock requests to populate TTI.
06:05 Maya: and step 3 uses a canary that respects cost buckets, so we don't route heavy batch workloads immediately. We throttle by QPS and by model-compute weight.
06:17 Elena: how do you simulate network partition vs capacity saturation — we want to test both.
06:21 Jordan: for partition we use a penalty of +500ms and force collision to see if fallback triggers; for capacity saturation we progressively decrease local capacity and verify routing moves to secondary region with minimal request loss.
06:34 Tom: what's the expected user-visible glitch during failover? A short 2–5s window of cold-responses then steady state?
06:40 Ravi: depends on warmstart. If we pre-warm top-10k prefixes it's under 1s for common sessions. No warmstart, expect 10–30s tail for uncommon sessions as KV warms and caches populate.
06:54 Priya: ops question — how to surface this in console? We need per-model per-region heatmap and warmstart progress.
07:01 Maya: Redwood Console exposes warmstart job progress, per-prefix hit rates, and a "failover health" indicator (latency, error rate, KV miss rate). We'll add an alert when KV miss rate crosses 10% post-failover.
07:15 Luis: on audit and compliance, we need immutable logs of what was routed and why for any DR event.
07:20 Jordan: we can export route decisions and policy versions; we also keep a policy change audit trail with who altered penalty thresholds. These exports are compatible with your SIEM.
07:33 Elena: can you summarize recommended default parameters for our environment? Our usual pattern: 60ms average latency target, 150ms 95th, mostly short prompts, some long-chat customers.
07:41 Maya: recommended defaults: geo-penalty +25ms additive, canary at 10% for 30min, pre-warm top-20k prefixes for the first minute after canary, batch window 6ms, quant-int8 for internal background jobs, int8 allowed for public endpoints with a +10ms model penalty in the score. Keep 4-bit only for non-critical workloads.
08:05 Ravi: also reserve burst capacity of 20% in secondary region for 15 minute windows so we don't oversubscribe during ramp.
08:12 Tom: let's talk instrumentation for the experiment — what data do you need from us?
08:16 Maya: per-route traffic distribution, model variant tags, historical top prefixes (top-100k), and latency SLOs by customer tier. Also an IAM role/key for our warmstart worker to write to your VPC endpoint.
08:28 Elena: security will sign off on scoped role. Luis will coordinate.
08:31 Luis: yes I'll need the principle of least privilege statement.
08:34 Jordan: we'll send the least-privilege template and IAM plan.
08:38 Priya: runbook timeline — can we do a small drill next Tuesday and a full two-region test the following week?
08:44 Jordan: yes we can schedule a 10% canary Tuesday at 16:00 UTC for 30 minutes. Full test Wed next week with warmstart seeding an hour before.
08:54 Elena: I want the cost delta estimate before Tuesday.
08:56 Jordan: understood.
09:00 Maya: quick note about sticky sessions — we support session affinity keys; during failover we translate affinity using a session-token reconciliation so clients keep continuity when possible. There's a corner case with long-lived streaming sessions that we do best-effort reconnection for.
09:18 Tom: reconnection loses streamed audio context for one chunk occasionally — documented?
09:22 Ravi: documented with example reconnect sequence; we'll share.
09:26 Maya: that covers most technicals — any last minute questions?
09:30 Elena: no, looks good. Thanks.
09:33 Jordan: recap and next steps in chat. We'll follow up with the runbook draft and the cost/latency matrix.

[End of recording — transcript may contain mis-attributed speaker segments and minor transcription errors]
